_readme: One entry per section (keyed by the section id in index.html). Each source is one video. 'videoId' is the YouTube id (the part after watch?v=). 'format': 'short' for YouTube Shorts. 'saltPct' drives the 'Calculate salt' button; leave it out for non-salt techniques. Method steps and key points take an optional 't' (seconds into the video) to show a timestamp button. Optional 'intro' is a short friendly line shown above the video. For recipe sections, set 'recipeLabel' on the section (e.g. 'quick pickle recipe') and 'cook' on each source (the name in the card header); 'tip' adds a 'Tip from <cook>' box. Non-recipe videos can also have 'context' (a short background note) and 'links' (a list of {text, url}, https only). Optional 'recipeTitle' replaces the generated card title; optional 'start' (seconds) is where the video starts when first played. A section can list 'filters' ([{id, label}]) and give each source a matching 'category' to show filter buttons above the thumbnails.

sources.title: Fermentation vs. Pickling: What's the Difference?
sources.creator: Wendy the Food Scientist
sources.intro: Here's Wendy the Food Scientist to explain it in under a minute.

points.text: Not all pickles are fermented, and not all fermented foods are pickles.
Lacto-fermentation: bacteria naturally present on the food turn its sugars into lactic acid over days to weeks, building complex flavour and probiotics that may benefit your gut.
Pickling: no fermentation, just vinegar added to make the food acidic. It tastes bright and fresh within a few hours.
Both methods bring the pH below 4.6, which stops harmful bacteria growing.

sources.fromDescription: her fermented dill pickles use a 2% salt brine, and her basic vinegar pickling brine is equal parts vinegar and water with 2 tbsp sugar and 1.5 tsp salt.

sources.title: The power of fermented foods
sources.creator: Health Hive
sources.intro: Here's neuroscientist Andrew Huberman on what happened when people ate more fermented food.

points.text: Huberman's advice: eat 2 to 4 servings of fermented foods a day, and mix up the kinds.
In the study he's describing, people's inflammatory markers went down.
Markers of autoimmune disruption went down too, and the chemistry of the gut shifted in a healthy direction.
That doesn't mean fibre is bad.

sources.context: About the study: Stanford researchers led by Justin and Erica Sonnenburg gave 36 healthy adults 10 weeks of either lots of fermented foods (yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, fermented vegetables, brine drinks and kombucha) or lots of fibre. The fermented-food group's gut microbes became more diverse and 19 inflammatory proteins in their blood went down, with bigger servings giving stronger effects. The high-fibre group saw neither change. The 2 to 4 servings a day is Huberman's everyday suggestion rather than a figure from the trial.

links.text: Full Huberman Lab episode with Dr Justin Sonnenburg

sources.title: How to make pickles like a chef
sources.creator: Fallow
sources.summary: Fallow, a London restaurant, makes crinkle-cut, restaurant-style cucumber pickles. The cucumbers are salted first to draw out water, then covered in a sweet and sharp brine of sugar, white wine vinegar and water, spiced with turmeric and mustard seed, and left for at least two days.
ingredients: Turmeric and mustard seed, or other whole spices

method.text: Slice the cucumbers. Fallow use a crinkle-cut knife for the classic pickle look.
Sprinkle with salt and leave for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, mix the pickling liquid: 1 part sugar, 3 parts white wine vinegar and 2 parts water.
Add turmeric and mustard seed, or try other spices for different flavours.
Rinse the cucumbers, pack them into a jar and pour over the pickling liquid.
Seal and leave for at least 2 days. The longer, the better.
Serve on burgers, as a garnish or as a snack.

sources.compare: This is a quick pickle: the jar isn't heat-processed, so keep it in the fridge. Half the liquid is vinegar, which gives a properly sharp pickle, and salting the slices first helps them stay crunchy.

sources.title: 2-day veggie pickle trick
sources.creator: Sivan's Kitchen
sources.summary: Sivan turns the leftover vegetables at the bottom of the fridge into crunchy pickles instead of throwing them away. Any mix of veg goes into a jar with salt, a splash of white vinegar and water, then sits on the counter for two days before moving to the fridge.
ingredients: Any vegetables you have, cut up. Sivan uses cabbage, cauliflower, cucumber, red pepper, jalapeños, celery, carrots, radishes and dill
2 tbsp kosher salt per 1 litre jar
About ½ cup (120 ml) white distilled vinegar per jar

method.text: Cut up whatever vegetables need using.
Wash them well.
Pack them tightly into clean jars, pressing down as you go. Recycled jars are fine.
Add 2 tbsp kosher salt and about ½ cup white vinegar to each 1 litre jar.
Top up with filtered water to the brim, seal tightly and give it a good shake.
Leave on the counter for 2 days, then move to the fridge to keep them cold and crisp.

sources.compare: This sits halfway between a quick pickle and a ferment: it uses less vinegar than a classic quick pickle, and two days at room temperature lets some fermentation get going. Keep every piece under the liquid, use a clean jar and move it to the fridge after the two days. Kosher salt varies a lot in weight, so weigh it if you can. The salt-only version is a ferment, so the Brine ferments advice applies.
sources.tip: For a salt-only version, skip the vinegar and add an extra ½ tbsp salt.

sources.title: Quick pickle cucumber
sources.creator: Andy Cooks
sources.summary: Andy's all-purpose quick pickle: equal parts vinegar and water with a spoonful each of salt and sugar, heated and poured over sliced cucumber with dill, chilli flakes and peppercorns. They're ready to eat as soon as they've cooled.
ingredients: Dill, chilli flakes and black peppercorns, or your own aromatics

method.text: Slice the cucumber.
Put it in a clean jar with the dill, peppercorns and chilli flakes.
Heat the vinegar, water, salt and sugar in a small pan until it simmers.
Pour the hot liquid over the cucumber.
Cover, leave to cool completely, then seal. They're ready to eat once cool.

sources.compare: A classic fridge pickle with a half-vinegar brine, which is about as sharp as quick pickles get. The jar isn't heat-processed, so keep it in the fridge and use clean utensils when you dip in.
sources.tip: The same liquid works for cauliflower, courgettes, radishes and even watermelon rind. The pickles keep in the fridge for up to six months.

sources.title: Quick pickle almost any vegetable with 2 ingredients
sources.creator: Bon Appétit
sources.summary: Chris Morocco's two-ingredient shortcut: thinly sliced vegetables tossed with a big pinch of salt and seasoned rice vinegar, which already contains sugar and salt. They're ready whenever you need them and keep for a few weeks.
ingredients: Seasoned rice vinegar (it already has sugar and salt in it)

method.text: Slice the vegetables thinly. Chris finds slicing quicker and easier than chopping.
Add a big pinch of salt and a good splash of seasoned rice vinegar.
Toss everything together.
Leave until you're ready to use them.

sources.compare: Less a jar pickle than a quick dressing: no water and no measuring. Seasoned rice vinegar is milder than white vinegar. Chris says they keep for a few weeks; store them covered in the fridge.

sources.title: Classic sauerkraut
sources.creator: Andy Cooks
sources.summary: Andy's classic sauerkraut: finely sliced green cabbage massaged with 2% salt until it gives up its juice, flavoured with caraway, then packed tight under its own brine in a glass jar and left to ferment for three weeks.
ingredients: Salt: 20 g for every 1 kg of sliced cabbage

method.text: Cut the cabbage in half, remove the core and slice it finely.
Weigh the sliced cabbage and weigh out 20 g of salt per kilo. Andy's 1.5 kg needs 30 g.
Working in batches, sprinkle on the salt and massage it in really well.
Leave it for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Mix in the caraway seeds, or leave it plain, and give it one last massage.
Choose a glass or ceramic jar, not plastic.
Pack the cabbage in really tightly and pour in all the brine from the bowl.
Weigh it down, put the lid on and leave it somewhere cool and dark for 3 weeks.
After 3 weeks it's ready. Keep it in the fridge from then on.

sources.tip: With an ordinary clip-top jar, open it every day to let the gas out, or it could burst. A water-lock lid lets the gas out by itself.
sources.compare: This matches tested guidance closely: 2% salt by weight is the standard for sauerkraut, and keeping it packed under its brine with a weight is what stops mould. Three weeks somewhere cool is on the slow side of the usual 1 to 4 weeks, which gives a deeper flavour. Taste it along the way and move it to the fridge when you like it.

sources.title: Traditional sauerkraut with carrot and dill
sources.creator: Capri Lilly
sources.summary: Capri's everyday sauerkraut: cabbage and carrot salted overnight so they release plenty of brine, flavoured with caraway and dill, then packed under an airlock and left for up to a month for a deeper, tangier flavour.
ingredients: 2 to 3 large carrots, shredded (she used 150 g)
Sea salt at 2 to 3% of the veg weight (she used 37 g, which is 3%). Avoid iodised salt and salt with anti-caking agents

method.text: Shred the cabbage thinly so it gives up its moisture more easily.
Weigh the cabbage and carrots, then work out the salt: 2 to 4%, using more if your kitchen is warm or you want a longer ferment.
Salt the cabbage, cover it and leave it overnight to soften and release plenty of brine.
Mix in the carrots, caraway and dill.
Pack it tightly into a jar, pressing out the air pockets, and weigh it down under the brine. Fit an airlock lid.
In the first week expect bubbles, cloudy brine and the veg pushing up. That's fermentation working, so keep pressing everything back under the brine.
Start tasting after about 2 weeks. Capri lets hers go a month for a richer flavour.
When it's ready, move it into smaller jars and keep it in the fridge.

sources.tip: An airlock lid lets the gas out by itself, so there's no daily burping and you can more or less make it and forget it.
sources.compare: Very close to tested guidance. Capri's 3% salt is a little higher than the usual 2%, which slows the ferment down and suits a warm kitchen or a long ferment. Leaving the salted cabbage overnight is fine, and her advice to avoid iodised salt matches Getting started.

sources.title: Pineapple, turmeric and ginger sauerkraut
sources.creator: Yang's Nourishing Kitchen
sources.summary: Yang's sweeter take on sauerkraut: cabbage salted until it releases its juice, then mixed with pineapple, fresh ginger and turmeric, packed tight and left somewhere cool and dark for at least 4 to 6 weeks. The video makes a quarter of her full recipe, enough for a 1 litre jar.
ingredients: 1 tbsp sea salt (Yang's rule is 1 tbsp for every 900 g of veg)

method.text: Shred the cabbage.
Massage the salt into the cabbage, then leave it for up to half a day until it has released its juice.
Mix in the pineapple, ginger and turmeric, plus the black pepper if you're using it.
Pack it into a jar as tightly as you can, pressing it down with a fork until the brine covers it. Leave 2 to 5 cm of space at the top.
Check it regularly, especially in the first 2 weeks: press it back down to release the bubbles and keep everything under the brine. Stand the jar on a plate to catch any overflow.
Leave it somewhere cool and dark for at least 4 to 6 weeks. Yang prefers 2 months or more.
Once it tastes how you like, move it to the fridge.

sources.tip: Don't add vinegar or water. Cabbage makes enough brine of its own, and vinegar can get in the way of the good bacteria.
sources.compare: Matches tested guidance on salt (about 2%) and on keeping everything under the brine. Yang's 4 to 6 week minimum is longer than most guides, which say 1 to 4 weeks; that's about flavour rather than safety, so taste earlier if you like. The pineapple adds extra sugar, so expect a lively start and keep a plate under the jar.

sources.title: Spiced parsnip sauerkraut
sources.creator: Gaz Oakley
sources.summary: Gaz's winter kraut swaps cabbage for grated parsnip, with apple for sweetness plus chilli, garlic, ginger, turmeric, garam masala and fennel seeds. It's salted at 2%, left for an hour to make its own brine, then packed down under a leaf and a weight to ferment.
ingredients: Ground turmeric, garam masala and fennel seeds
Sea salt: 2% of the weight of everything in the bowl

method.text: Peel and grate the parsnips into a big mixing bowl.
Add finely chopped apple for sweetness, then chilli, garlic and ginger.
Add your herbs, then the spices: ground turmeric, garam masala and fennel seeds.
Weigh everything in the bowl, add 2% of that weight in sea salt and mix really well.
Leave it for about an hour so the salt draws out the moisture and makes a natural brine.
Pack it into clean jars, pressing down until the brine covers everything.
Lay a large leaf over the top and add a weight so nothing floats up.
Seal the jar and stand it on a plate to ferment.

sources.compare: Same 2% salt as a classic sauerkraut, so the calculator works as it is. Gaz doesn't give quantities or a fermenting time, so mix the veg and spices to taste and follow Getting started: taste from about day 5 and move it to the fridge when you like it. If you seal it with an ordinary lid, open it daily to let the gas out.

sources.title: Noma guide to lacto-fermented pickles
sources.creator: Ethan Chlebowski
sources.summary: Ethan walks through the method used at Noma, the Copenhagen restaurant, for fermenting almost any vegetable in brine: weigh the veg and water together, add exactly 2% of that weight in salt, keep everything under the brine and start tasting after 2 or 3 days.

glance.Where: Room temp, out of the sun

ingredients: Cucumbers, or any vegetable that's good raw, juicy and firm. Avoid waxed veg; organic if you can
Salt: 2% of the combined weight of veg and water
Optional: bay leaves, mustard seeds, peppercorns, chilli, garlic

method.text: Give the veg a light rinse but don't scrub it: the bacteria you need live on the skin.
Put the empty jar on the scales and zero it, then fit the veg in snugly with any spices.
Add water to cover and note the weight. Ethan's came to 414 g.
Weigh out 2% of that in salt. Pour the water off, dissolve the salt in it and pour it back over.
Screw the lid on loosely, about two-finger tight, so gas can escape. Weigh down anything that floats, for example with a water-filled zip-lock bag.
Leave at room temperature out of direct sunlight. If it gets very fizzy, open the lid to let the gas out.
Start tasting after 2 to 3 days. When it's sour enough, tighten the lid and move it to the fridge, where it keeps for several months.

sources.tip: You can go above 2% salt, but never below it.
sources.compare: This is exactly how the Pickle Hub brine calculator works, so set it to 2%. Ethan's food-safety points match tested guidance: there's no need to sterilise jars, fuzzy mould means throw it out, a flat white film (kahm yeast) can be skimmed off, and the bacteria that cause botulism can't grow below pH 4.6.

sources.title: The most helpful fermentation guide
sources.creator: LifebyMikeG
sources.summary: A masterclass in two-ingredient ferments: vegetables, salt and water. Mike explains how to choose a salt level between 2 and 5% of the total weight, then ferments carrots and beets at 3.5%, along with garlic scapes, turnips and radish pods from his garden.
ingredients: Carrots and beets, or any firm veg, chopped into bite-sized pieces
Salt: 3.5% of the combined weight of veg and water

method.text: Peel shop-bought veg, since you don't know what it's been treated with, and cut off any blemishes. Chop into bite-sized pieces.
Put a clean jar on the scales, zero it, add the veg and cover with water.
Multiply the weight of veg and water by 0.035 to get the salt. Weigh it out and add it.
Put the lid on and shake to get the salt dissolving.
Add a glass weight to keep everything under the water line.
Fit a one-way airlock lid, or use an ordinary lid and open it regularly to let the gas out.
Leave out of sunlight at 15 to 24°C. Cooler is slower and easier to control.
Taste after about 5 days. The first few days can taste a bit off; it keeps getting better with time.

sources.tip: Choosing your salt: go higher, up to 5%, for long ferments, dense veg like beets and carrots, or if you're a beginner. Go lower, down to 2%, for quick ferments, softer veg like radishes, or a more fermented flavour.
sources.compare: Mike measures salt against the total weight of veg and water, just like the Pickle Hub calculator, so the button below gives the right amount. His 2 to 5% range and 15 to 24°C match tested guidance, and he's clear that anything that grows mould after floating above the brine should be thrown away.

sources.title: Fermented tomatoes
sources.creator: DishByDavid
sources.summary: Firm Roma tomatoes fermented whole in brine until they turn bold and tangy. David's tricks: clean the skins, prick the stem ends so the brine gets inside, and scatter mustard seeds over the top. They're ready when the skins peel off easily.
ingredients: Brine (salt and water). David doesn't give his strength in the video

method.text: Rinse the tomatoes with a little bicarbonate of soda to clean the skins.
Prick the stem end of each tomato a couple of times with a toothpick so the brine soaks right in.
Pack them into a jar and cover with brine.
Sprinkle mustard seeds over the top.
Leave for a few days. They're ready when the skins peel off easily.

sources.compare: David doesn't give a salt strength in the video; his full recipe is in a paid guide. Getting started suggests 3.5% of the water (35 g salt per litre) as an all-purpose brine. Mustard seeds add flavour, but they're no substitute for keeping the tomatoes under the brine, so weigh them down if they float.

sources.title: Fermented lemons
sources.creator: Capri Lilly
sources.summary: Moroccan-style preserved lemons: lemons cut into quarters, packed with salt into a jar until they're covered in their own juice, then left at room temperature for 3 to 4 weeks. The softened rinds add a salty, tangy depth to dressings, grains, chicken and more.

glance.Salt: About ½ cup per 1 litre jar

ingredients: 6 to 10 lemons for a 1 litre jar, organic or unwaxed if you can
About ½ cup coarse sea salt or kosher salt, plus more as needed
Extra freshly squeezed lemon juice for topping up (not bottled)
Optional spices: cinnamon sticks, star anise, cloves, thyme, bay leaves

method.text: Cut a little off the small ends so each lemon stands flat.
Cut each lemon into quarters without cutting through the base, so it opens like a flower.
Pack salt generously into each lemon, getting it into every gap.
Press the lemons tightly into a clean jar, adding a few teaspoons of salt between layers and pressing down to release their juice.
If there isn't enough juice to cover them, top up with fresh lemon juice. Add any leftover salt and a fermentation weight.
Seal and leave at room temperature for 3 to 4 weeks. For the first week or two, turn the jar upside down once a day.
They're ready when the rinds are soft. Rinse them before using to take the edge off the salt.

sources.tip: It's mostly the rind and pith you use, finely chopped. Try them in dressings, hummus, grain bowls and roast veg, or with chicken, fish or lamb.
sources.compare: Capri sterilises her jars by boiling them for 20 minutes. That isn't needed for ferments, and boiling can crack glass (see Getting started): a jar washed in hot, soapy water is fine. This is a very salty ferment, which is why it keeps so long, and why the lemons need a rinse before you eat them.

sources.title: Lacto-fermented stone fruit
sources.creator: Capri Lilly
sources.summary: Peaches, plums and nectarines covered in a 2% salt water brine and left for 3 to 7 days, tasting daily until they're as tangy as you like. The result is sweet, sour and savoury: good on a cheese board, with yoghurt or with grilled meat.
ingredients: Stone fruit: peaches, plums or nectarines
Salt for a 2% brine: 20 g per litre of water

method.text: Put the fruit in a clean jar and cover it with a 2% salt water brine (20 g salt per litre of water).
Leave it to ferment for 3 to 7 days, opening the jar to let the gas out and tasting it every day.
When it's tangy enough for you, move it to the fridge, where it keeps for about 2 months.

sources.compare: A 2% brine is on the gentle side, which suits a quick ferment. Fruit is sugary, so it ferments fast: taste daily as Capri says, and keep the fruit under the brine with a weight. Her brine is 2% of the water only, so use 20 g per litre rather than the calculator, which counts the fruit too.

sources.title: Traditional kimchi (tongbaechu-kimchi)
sources.creator: Maangchi
sources.summary: Maangchi's traditional whole-cabbage kimchi: napa cabbage salted for two hours and rinsed, then every leaf spread with a paste of sweet rice porridge, chilli flakes, garlic, ginger, onion, fish sauce, salted shrimp, radish and spring onions. It sits out for a day or two to start fermenting, then goes in the fridge.
ingredients: For the porridge: 2 cups water, 2 tbsp sweet (glutinous) rice flour and 2 tbsp brown sugar
½ cup minced garlic, 2 tsp minced ginger and 1 cup minced onion
¼ cup salted fermented shrimp (saeujeot), chopped
1 to 2½ cups Korean chilli flakes (gochugaru): about 1 cup for mild, 2 for spicy
About 2 cups Korean radish, cut into matchsticks
Spring onions, plus Asian chives and minari if you can find them

method.text: Trim the cabbage, cut a slit in the base and tear it in half by hand so the leaves stay whole.
Dunk the halves in cold water, then sprinkle the salt between the leaves, using more on the thick stems.
Leave for 2 hours, turning it every 30 minutes so it salts evenly.
Meanwhile, make the porridge: simmer the water and rice flour, stirring, until it thickens. Stir in the brown sugar and let it cool completely.
Mix the cooled porridge with the garlic, ginger, onion, fish sauce, chopped shrimp and chilli flakes, then stir in the radish and spring onions.
Rinse the salted cabbage three times in fresh cold water and drain it really well.
Spread the paste between every leaf. Wear gloves if it's your first time, because the chilli stings.
Pack it into a jar or container, pressing down to push out the air, and close the lid.
Leave at room temperature for a day or two, until it smells sour and starts to bubble, then move it to the fridge.
As it ferments, keep pressing it down so it stays under its own juice.

sources.tip: Eat some straight away as fresh kimchi (geotjeori), torn up with sesame seeds and warm rice, while the rest ferments.
sources.compare: Kimchi is salted differently from sauerkraut: the cabbage is soaked in salt and then rinsed, so there's no weighed percentage and the calculator doesn't apply. A day or two at room temperature and then the fridge is the usual way to make it. Leave room in the jar for the juice to rise, and keep the kimchi pressed under it.

sources.title: How to make kimchi like a Korean
sources.creator: Johnny Kyunghwo
sources.summary: A quicker, cut-up kimchi: the cabbage is chopped before salting, softened for a few hours or overnight, rinsed and wrung out, then tossed with radish, spring onions and a rice-flour paste of garlic, onion, fish sauce and chilli flakes. Two days on the counter, then into the fridge.
ingredients: 1 onion and 15 to 20 cloves of garlic
Sea salt, for salting the cabbage

method.text: Remove the tough outer leaves, then cut a cross in the base and split the cabbage into quarters by hand.
Chop the quarters lengthwise into pieces and put them in a large pot.
Sprinkle with sea salt and leave for a few hours, or overnight, to soften. The exact amount doesn't matter much because it gets rinsed off, but don't overdo it.
Cut the radish into sticks and the spring onions into similar lengths.
Blend the onion and garlic into a paste, adding a splash of fish sauce to help it blend.
Whisk the water and rice flour in a small pan and bring to the boil, stirring constantly, until thick.
Stir in the garlic paste, then add chilli flakes until the paste is thick enough to cling to the cabbage. Let it cool.
Rinse the cabbage under fresh water and wring out as much water as you can, twice.
Toss the cabbage with the radish and spring onions, then put on gloves and mix in the cooled paste until everything is evenly coated. Taste, and add more fish sauce, salt or chilli if you like.
Pack it into a glass jar, pressing down as you go. Lay plastic wrap on top to keep the air off, then close the lid.
Leave on the counter for about 2 days, then move it to the fridge, where it keeps fermenting slowly.

sources.tip: Don't overfill the jar: kimchi ferments fast and the juice can overflow. Johnny uses any leftover paste to make a quick radish kimchi.
sources.compare: Like Maangchi's, the salt is rinsed off, so there's no percentage to measure. Johnny's 2 days out and then the fridge matches hers. If you use an airtight jar, open it every day or two to let the gas out.

sources.title: Cucumber kimchi (oi kimchi)
sources.creator: Aaron and Claire
sources.summary: The easiest kimchi there is: cucumber pieces with the watery seeds scooped out, salted briefly to keep them crunchy, then gently tossed with a quick paste of chilli flakes, fish sauce, garlic, ginger and sugar, plus spring onions. A few hours on the counter, then into the fridge, where it keeps for a few weeks.

glance.Keeps: A few weeks, in the fridge

ingredients: 2 tbsp coarse sea salt (or about 1 tbsp fine salt)
A big handful of spring onions, cut into 5 cm strips (or garlic chives)
6 cloves garlic (about 2 tbsp), very finely chopped

method.text: Trim the ends off the cucumbers and cut them into quarters lengthwise.
Scrape out the watery seeds with a spoon, so the kimchi stays crisp and doesn't go watery.
Cut into bite-sized pieces.
Toss with the coarse sea salt and leave for 10 minutes.
Drain in a colander for 20 minutes, then rinse in cold water. Taste a piece and rinse again if it's too salty.
Cut the spring onions into strips, chop the garlic very finely and grate the ginger.
Mix the chilli flakes, fish sauce, garlic, ginger and sugar into a paste.
In a big bowl, gently toss the drained cucumbers with the paste, then add the spring onions. Be gentle: squeezing makes it watery.
Taste, and add a little more fish sauce if you'd like it saltier.
Eat it straight away, or for a better flavour leave it at room temperature for 3 to 4 hours, then keep it in the fridge.

sources.tip: Don't add vinegar. Kimchi gets its sourness from fermenting, not from vinegar.
sources.compare: This is a quick, lightly fermented kimchi: a few hours out and then the fridge, so it starts fresh and slowly turns sour over the following weeks. As with cabbage kimchi, the salt is rinsed off, so there's no percentage to weigh. Scooping out the seeds and salting first is what keeps it crunchy.

sources.title: Kimchi-style courgette ferment
sources.creator: Gaz Oakley
sources.summary: Gaz's answer to a glut of courgettes: chunks tossed with spring onions, lots of garlic, soy sauce, seaweed flakes, honey and Korean chilli flakes, salted at 2% to make their own brine, then packed down and left for about a week until tangy and a little fizzy.
ingredients: Courgettes, or a marrow, cut into large chunks
Sea salt: 2% of the weight of everything in the bowl

method.text: Chop the courgettes into large chunks and put them in a mixing bowl.
Add the spring onions and plenty of garlic.
For umami and sweetness, add soy sauce, seaweed flakes and a little honey.
Add the Korean chilli flakes.
Weigh everything in the bowl and add 2% of that weight in sea salt.
Mix really well and leave for about 2 hours until plenty of brine has formed.
Pack it tightly into a jar and press everything down under the brine.
Plug the top with a couple of leaves and add a fermentation weight.
Label with the date and leave at room temperature for about a week.
When it's tangy and a little fizzy, move it to the fridge, where it keeps for a very long time.

sources.compare: This uses the same 2% total-weight method as the Pickle Hub calculator. It's fish-free: soy sauce and seaweed give it savoury depth instead. Gaz sterilises his jar, which isn't necessary; a clean jar washed in hot, soapy water is fine.

sources.title: Lemon and mandarin cheong
sources.creator: Johnny Kyunghwo
sources.summary: Cheong is a Korean fruit syrup made by packing fruit in an equal weight of sugar. Johnny slices lemons and mandarins thinly, buries them in sugar and leaves the jar on the counter until the sugar dissolves, then keeps it in the fridge. A spoonful in hot water makes a soothing citrus tea.
ingredients: Lemons, washed well to remove any wax
Sugar: the same weight as the fruit

method.text: Wash the lemons well to get rid of any waxy coating.
Halve the lemons and slice them as thinly as you can, ideally on a mandoline. Peel and thinly slice the mandarins.
Weigh the fruit, then weigh out the same weight of sugar.
Mix about two-thirds of the sugar thoroughly into the fruit.
Pack it into a jar and cover with the rest of the sugar.
Leave it on the counter until the sugar has dissolved. Johnny's took about 2 days.
Keep it in the fridge. Stir a spoonful into hot water or tea.

sources.compare: Cheong is preserved mainly by sugar: an equal weight of sugar draws out the juice and keeps spoilage at bay. Left somewhere warm it can start to ferment, so once the sugar has dissolved, keep it in the fridge. Use a clean, dry jar and keep the fruit covered with syrup so it doesn't go mouldy.

sources.title: Every cheong syrup I made in 2023
sources.creator: Johnny Kyunghwo
sources.summary: A year of cheong experiments, all made the same simple way: cranberry, red onion, tomato and basil, fresh bay leaf, strawberry, blueberry, plum, peach, chilli and yuja (yuzu). The fruit, veg or herbs are weighed, mixed with an equal weight of sugar and left until they turn into a syrup.

glance.Time: A night to a few weeks

ingredients: Fruit, veg or herbs of your choice, washed and dried
Sugar (white or organic cane): the same weight as the fruit

method.text: Wash and dry the fruit thoroughly, and pick out any bruised or very soft pieces.
Cut it up so the sugar can draw out the juice faster. Whole berries take much longer.
Weigh it, then weigh out the same weight of sugar.
Mix in about two-thirds of the sugar, pack it into a clean jar and top with the rest.
Leave it on the counter for a night to a few days, then move it to the fridge. Soft, juicy fruit can go straight into the fridge.
When the sugar has dissolved, strain off the syrup. The leftover fruit can be dried and used as a garnish.

sources.tip: Frozen fruit works too: let it thaw completely, then use the usual equal weight of sugar.
sources.compare: Johnny's first cranberry cheong went mouldy because the whole berries floated above the syrup. His advice: stir it regularly, keep everything submerged and use the fridge, especially for soft, juicy fruit. If you don't want it to ferment, refrigerate it once the sugar has dissolved.

sources.title: How to easily start making kombucha
sources.creator: Johnny Kyunghwo
sources.summary: How to start kombucha without buying a scoby: brew black tea, sweeten it with 10% of its weight in sugar, let it cool, then add some raw, unpasteurised kombucha. Cover it with a cloth and wait for a new scoby to grow on top.
ingredients: Sugar: 10% of the weight of the brewed tea (Johnny's 1,180 g of tea took 118 g)
Raw, unpasteurised kombucha, shop-bought or from a friend, or a scoby with its liquid

method.text: Bring the water to the boil, turn off the heat, add the tea bags and let them steep for about 10 minutes.
Strain the tea into a jug on the scales so you know its weight.
Add sugar at 10% of the tea's weight and stir until it dissolves.
Let it cool completely to room temperature. An ice bath speeds this up.
Pour it into a clean glass jar and add the raw kombucha, or a scoby with its liquid.
Cover with a cloth or kitchen paper and leave it undisturbed at room temperature.
A layer of jelly forms on top: that's your new scoby. Once it's thick and the tea tastes a little vinegary, use them to start the next batch.

sources.tip: Black tea is best while you're growing a new scoby. Johnny switches to green tea once he's brewing kombucha to drink.
sources.compare: Starting from raw kombucha works because the liquid brings the yeasts and bacteria and makes the tea acidic from the start. Brew in glass, cover with a breathable cloth to keep flies out, and throw out any batch that grows fuzzy mould.

sources.title: Kombucha masterclass
sources.creator: Gaz Oakley
sources.summary: Gaz's whole kombucha method in under two minutes: brew loose black tea, sweeten and dilute it, add a scoby with a cup of mature kombucha and leave it for 7 to 10 days. Then bottle it with fruit and herbs for a second fermentation that makes it fizzy.
ingredients: 2.5 litres filtered water for brewing, plus 2.5 litres cool water
Loose black tea (Gaz uses Assam) or tea bags
A scoby with about a cup of mature kombucha
Fruit and herbs for flavouring, such as blackberries and mint, or rhubarb and strawberries

method.text: Bring 2.5 litres of filtered water to the boil and add the black tea.
Turn off the heat, steep for 10 to 15 minutes, then stir in the sugar.
Pour into a clean fermentation jar (one with a tap is handy) and add 2.5 litres of cool water to bring it to room temperature.
Add the scoby and about a cup of mature kombucha.
Cover with muslin and leave for 7 to 10 days.
Taste from day 7. If it's still too sweet, give it longer; when it's pleasantly tangy, it's ready.
Bottle it plain or with fruit and herbs, leaving a little space at the top.
Seal and leave at room temperature for 3 to 5 days to build up fizz, then move the bottles to the fridge.

sources.tip: You can buy a scoby and starter liquid online, or ask a friend who already brews.
sources.compare: Gaz doesn't give a sugar amount; Johnny's 10% of the tea's weight is a good guide. The second fermentation builds pressure in sealed bottles, so use bottles designed for fizzy drinks, leave space at the top and open one after a couple of days to check.

sources.title: Make any probiotic soda from ginger
sources.creator: Whole Shenanigans
sources.summary: A ginger bug is a homemade starter for fizzy drinks: grated ginger, sugar and water, fed every day until it bubbles. Add a spoonful of its liquid to almost any juice, bottle it, and within a day or so you have a naturally fizzy soda.

glance.Ratio: 1 tbsp bug per cup of juice

ingredients: Organic ginger, grated (no need to peel)
Sugar: organic cane or plain white
Non-chlorinated water: filtered, spring, or tap water left out for 24 hours
Juice for the soda, at room temperature and without preservatives

method.text: Wash and grate the ginger. Organic ginger doesn't need peeling.
In a clean glass jar, mix 2 cups of water with 2 tbsp sugar and 2 tbsp grated ginger.
Cover loosely with a cloth or paper towel. Unlike most ferments, a ginger bug needs a little air.
Feed it every day with another 2 tbsp each of sugar and ginger, and give it a stir.
After about 5 days it should be bubbling. It's happiest at 21 to 24°C.
To make soda, strain 1 tbsp of the bug's liquid into a swing-top bottle for every cup of juice.
Top up with juice, leaving 2.5 to 5 cm of space at the top, and seal.
Leave at room temperature for 12 hours to about 3 days, opening it at least once a day to let the gas out.

sources.tip: Skip raw honey and non-fermentable sugars. Honey's natural antimicrobials can stop the bug getting going.
sources.compare: Opening the bottles every day matters: swing-top bottles can build enough pressure to burst. Once it's as fizzy as you like, move it to the fridge to slow things down.

sources.title: Brad makes tepache
sources.creator: Bon Appétit
sources.summary: Tepache is a lightly fermented Mexican pineapple drink. Brad packs a whole pineapple, skin and all, into a jar with brown sugar, ginger, habanero, cinnamon and water, leaves it for a few days, then bottles it for a couple more to make it fizzy.

glance.Sugar: About a cup of brown sugar

ingredients: 1 ripe pineapple, not washed: the skin carries useful yeasts
A knob of fresh ginger, crushed
A habanero or other chilli, ends trimmed

method.text: Use a large jar that seals. Brad rigs his with a rubber band so it lets out excess pressure.
Wash the ginger, trim the tips and crush it.
Trim the ends off the chilli and open it up. There's no need to chop it.
Cut the top and bottom off the pineapple without washing it, quarter it, trim off a little of the core and cut it into chunks.
Add the brown sugar and a little water and shake to dissolve.
Add the rest of the pineapple and the cinnamon, muddle it down and top up with a splash more water.
Leave at room temperature for a few days until it's bubbling.
Strain, then bottle in proper fermentation bottles, leaving 2.5 cm of space at the top.
Leave the bottles for 2 to 3 days to carbonate, then chill before opening.
For a second batch, add water and 2 tbsp brown sugar to the leftover pineapple.

sources.tip: Only use bottles made for fermenting. Decorative glass bottles can explode under the pressure.
sources.compare: Tepache is a quick ferment driven mostly by wild yeasts, which is why it smells a little beery. The unwashed pineapple skin supplies them, but rinse off any visible dirt. Pineapple and ginger build fizz fast, so check the bottles daily and keep them in the fridge once they're carbonated.

sources.title: Fruit kvass
sources.creator: Adam Witt
sources.summary: A way to rescue leftover fruit: put it in a jar with water and a little sugar and leave it on the counter for 3 to 5 days until it turns lightly fizzy. Fruit kvass is an old Eastern European drink, a sort of homemade soda from before soda existed.

method.text: Put the leftover fruit in a jar with water and some sugar.
Leave it on the counter at room temperature for 3 to 5 days.
Drink it as it is, freeze it into ice lollies, or use it as a mixer.

sources.compare: Adam doesn't give amounts or say how to cover the jar. Use a clean jar, cover it loosely or open it daily to let the gas out, and move it to the fridge once it's fizzy. Throw it out if it grows fuzzy mould.
